explanations.answer: Go glean grain in the fields
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, this one is Ruth's idea. She tells Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, "Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor." Gleaning just means picking up grain behind the harvesters. Naomi doesn't hand her a plan. Ruth walks in with her own.

explanations.answer: Find work in the town market
explanations.explanation: A market stall sounds reasonable, baker, but Ruth never mentions one. What she asks for is to go into the fields. She wants to glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight she may find favor.

Ruth is not asking to leave, friend. The foreman says she is the one "…who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab." (Ruth 2:6), and Ruth asks to go into the fields. Moab is where she came from, and Boaz later says she left the land of her birth (Ruth 2:11). Today she is heading for the grain.
Naomi doesn't tell her to stay home, friend. After Ruth shares her plan, Naomi answers, "Go ahead, my daughter…" That is a yes. Ruth gets her blessing before she walks out the door.
Right, baker. Ruth the Moabitess asks to go glean, and Naomi replies, "Go ahead, my daughter…" That is a yes. Ruth heads out into the field.

That's the one, friend. The text says Ruth "…happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech." Elimelech was Naomi's husband (Ruth 1:2-3), so Boaz is family. Ruth just happened to land in his part.

Gideon is a name from another part of the Bible, in the book of Judges (Judges 6:11), but he isn't in this field. Ruth comes to the part belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech. Boaz is the name to hold onto, baker.

Nabal is a man from a different story, way over in 1 Samuel 25:3, so he's nowhere near this barley. The field Ruth reaches belongs to Boaz, from the clan of Elimelech. Different story, different man, baker.
Not quite, friend. Boaz asks his foreman, "Whose young woman is this?" The foreman answers him. Boaz speaks to Ruth herself after that.
That's right, baker. Boaz turns to the foreman of his harvesters and asks, "Whose young woman is this?" The question goes to the foreman, not to Ruth. Then the foreman tells him who she is.

explanations.answer: Since morning with one short rest
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The foreman says she "…has continued from morning until now, except that she rested a short time in the shelter." That is steady work with one short rest. Boaz hears all of it before he speaks to her.

explanations.answer: Only since the middle of the day
explanations.explanation: Ruth started earlier than that, friend. The foreman says she has continued "…from morning until now…" The only pause he mentions is a short rest in the shelter. She has been at it a good while.

explanations.answer: Just a few minutes so far
explanations.explanation: A few minutes? Friend, that's me stirring one bowl of dough and calling it a workout. The foreman says Ruth has continued "…from morning until now…" with one short rest in the shelter. That is real work.
Yes, baker, field. Boaz says, "Do not go and glean in another field…" and he tells her to stay close to his servant girls. He keeps her right there in his own field. Ruth gets a place to stay put.
Not town, friend. Ruth is already out in the grain, so Boaz's word is about the field. He says, "Do not go and glean in another field…" Then he adds that she should stay close to his servant girls.
Country is a big jump, baker. Boaz keeps it small and says, "Do not go and glean in another field…" He wants her right there by his servant girls. One field, one spot.
Yes, baker. Boaz tells her, "Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you." The order is already given before she even asks. I think that is a man looking out for her.
It's actually true, friend. Boaz tells Ruth, "Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you." He has already told his young men. Ruth hears it straight from him.

explanations.answer: Drink from the jars the young men filled
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Boaz says, "…when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled." Somebody else already did the hauling. All Ruth has to do is walk over and drink.

explanations.answer: Walk back into town for a drink
explanations.explanation: A walk back to town isn't part of the offer, friend. Boaz tells her, "…when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled." The young men already filled those jars. Boaz points her to them.

explanations.answer: Draw water from the well herself
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't have to do that, baker. Boaz says, "…go and drink from the jars the young men have filled." The young men already filled them. Nobody asks her to draw a drop.

explanations.answer: Why he would take notice of a foreigner
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Ruth asks, "Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?" She is a Moabitess in Israel's field, and she asks it with her face to the ground. Her question is honest and humble.

explanations.answer: Whether Naomi can glean here too
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't ask that, friend. She asks why Boaz has taken notice of her, "…even though I am a foreigner?" The question is about herself and his favor. Naomi comes up later, when Boaz answers.

explanations.answer: What she owes him for the water
explanations.explanation: Ruth never mentions a bill, baker. She asks, "Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?" Her question is about why he noticed her at all. The water isn't what she's asking about.

Yes, baker. Boaz says he has been made fully aware of "…all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband…" That mother-in-law is Naomi. Word about Ruth had already reached him.
Not a sister-in-law, friend. Boaz says he knows "…all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband…" His words are about Naomi. Ruth's care for her is what he has heard about.

Her father shows up in the next breath, friend, but not as the answer. Boaz says he knows what she did for her mother-in-law, and then adds that she "…left your father and mother and the land of your birth…" So her parents were part of what she left behind. The one she took care of is her mother-in-law.

That's right, baker. Boaz says, "May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge." The wings belong to the LORD. Ruth came to a people she did not know, and Boaz says she took refuge with Him.

Boaz is from that clan, friend, but he doesn't point to it here. He says Ruth has taken refuge under the wings of "…the LORD, the God of Israel…" The refuge is with Him. A clan has no wings in this verse.
The elders aren't in this scene, baker. Boaz speaks of "…the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge." That is whose wings they are. Look for the LORD in that line.
Yes, baker. The text says Ruth "…ate and was satisfied and had some left over." A full belly plus a portion to spare. I've never seen a better meal.
She had plenty, friend. Verse 14 says she "…ate and was satisfied and had some left over." So she finished eating and still had some to spare. Remember that leftover part, because it comes up again.
It's the opposite, baker. Boaz orders his young men, "Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her." That is a rule for how they treat her. She is allowed to gather there.

That's right, friend. Boaz tells his young men, "Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her." It's an order, and it's about how they speak to Ruth. She can gather there without being insulted.

explanations.answer: Pull out stalks from the bundles for her
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Boaz says, "Rather, pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather." Then he adds, "Do not rebuke her." It's like a teammate leaving the ball right where you can reach it.

explanations.answer: Carry all of her grain into town
explanations.explanation: Boaz doesn't offer a delivery service, friend. He tells his young men to pull out some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather. Ruth still does the gathering. His order just makes her work go further.

explanations.answer: Give her a share of their own wages
explanations.explanation: No paychecks in this scene, baker. Boaz says, "…pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather." The help comes as stalks in the field. Wages never come up.
Barley it is, baker. After Ruth beats out what she gleaned, it comes to "…about an ephah of barley." An ephah is a measure for grain. That's a solid day's work.
Spelt is a grain, friend, but it isn't the one named here. The text says Ruth's gleanings came to "…about an ephah of barley." Barley is the word to put in the blank.

Millet is a good guess, baker, but the verse says barley. Ruth beats out what she gleaned, and it comes to "…about an ephah of barley." An ephah is a measure for grain. Same measure, different grain than millet.

explanations.answer: What she saved from her meal
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, that's the one. Ruth "…brought out what she had saved from her meal and gave it to Naomi." That is the food left over from verse 14. There she "…ate and was satisfied and had some left over." She didn't come home with only grain.

explanations.answer: A gift of silver from Boaz
explanations.explanation: Silver would be a fun plot twist, baker, but there's none in this chapter. The text says Ruth brought out "…what she had saved from her meal…" That's the food left over from her meal in verse 14. She gives it to Naomi.

explanations.answer: A water jar from the field
explanations.explanation: Not a jar, friend. Ruth picks up the grain and brings out "…what she had saved from her meal…" for Naomi. What she carries is grain and her saved food. Boaz's jars were for her to drink from (Ruth 2:9).

Yes, baker. Naomi says, "Blessed be the man who noticed you." and only after that does Ruth tell her, "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz…" Naomi blesses him first. She didn't even have his name yet.
Order matters here, friend. Naomi says, "Blessed be the man who noticed you." and that is before Ruth names Boaz. She blesses a man she hasn't heard a name for yet. Then Ruth tells her it's Boaz.

explanations.answer: He is one of their kinsman-redeemers
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Naomi says, "The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers." She says it right after Ruth tells her his name. Family is the piece to hold onto.

explanations.answer: He is a priest at the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: The text never calls Boaz a priest, friend. Naomi says, "The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers." What she stresses is family, close family.

explanations.answer: He is a judge over all Israel
explanations.explanation: Boaz is a prominent man, baker, but he is never called a judge. Naomi says, "The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers." That's how she describes him. It's all about being family.

explanations.answer: Until they finish gathering all his harvest
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ruth tells Naomi, "Stay with my young men until they have finished gathering all my harvest." The time is tied to the harvest being finished. No week or day is named.

explanations.answer: Until the end of this one week
explanations.explanation: A week isn't what Ruth reports, friend. She tells Naomi, "Stay with my young men until they have finished gathering all my harvest." The time is tied to the harvest. Nobody mentions a week.

explanations.answer: Until the next Sabbath day comes
explanations.explanation: No Sabbath in these words, baker. Ruth repeats Boaz this way: "Stay with my young men until they have finished gathering all my harvest." It lasts as long as the harvest does.

explanations.answer: So nothing will happen to her in another field
explanations.explanation: That's what Naomi says, baker. "My daughter, it is good for you to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to you in another field." It's Naomi's own reason, right in her words. Ruth stays put after that.

explanations.answer: So Boaz will pay her a fair wage
explanations.explanation: Pay never comes up, friend. Naomi says, "…it is good for you to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to you in another field." Her concern is what could happen to Ruth in another field.

explanations.answer: So she can learn the customs of Israel
explanations.explanation: Customs aren't mentioned here, baker. Naomi says it is good for Ruth to work with his young women "…so that nothing will happen to you in another field." That is the whole reason she gives.

She stays longer than that, friend. The text says Ruth stayed close to the servant girls of Boaz "…until the barley and wheat harvests were finished." That is two harvests, not one. It's a longer stretch than most people keep a New Year's promise.

Right, baker. Ruth stays close to Boaz's servant girls "…until the barley and wheat harvests were finished." The passage names both the barley harvest and the wheat harvest. She keeps at it through both.
